articles.title: Denver Broncos cheerleader’s secret day job has fans completely amazed
articles.summary: NFL cheerleaders are known for balancing demanding schedules, but few stories have captured fans’ attention quite like that of Denver Broncos cheerleader Ann-Marie Muscarello.
articles.body:
NFL cheerleaders are known for balancing demanding schedules, but few stories have captured fans’ attention quite like that of Denver Broncos cheerleader Ann-Marie Muscarello.

Over the past several days, Muscarello has gone viral on social media after football fans discovered that her life extends far beyond the sidelines of Broncos games.

While many know her as one of the faces of Denver’s cheerleading squad on Sundays, her primary profession during the week is one that carries a very different kind of responsibility: she is a nurse.

The revelation has sparked admiration across social media, with fans praising Muscarello for successfully navigating two careers that demand energy, discipline, and an unwavering commitment to helping others.

articles.title: Broncos cheerleader’s double life reignites heated debate over low NFL pay
articles.standfirst: The Broncos cheerleader’s demanding schedule is highlighting a long-running debate over NFL cheerleader compensation
articles.summary: The Broncos cheerleader’s demanding schedule is highlighting a long-running debate over NFL cheerleader compensation
articles.body:
Denver Broncos cheerleader Ann-Marie Muscarello is giving NFL fans a glimpse into the demanding reality behind the glamour of professional football.

The veteran cheerleader recently shared a social media post showing the striking contrast between her Sundays on the sidelines and her Mondays working as an orthopedic nurse.

“Sunday mornings vs. Monday mornings look a little different,” Muscarello wrote on Instagram, alongside images highlighting her two very different careers. The post quickly attracted attention, with fans praising her work ethic while also questioning why NFL cheerleaders often need another job to make ends meet.

Many commenters described Muscarello as inspiring and impressive, particularly because she manages the physical demands of professional cheerleading while working in healthcare during the week.

Others focused on the financial side of the situation, arguing that women who dedicate their time to NFL franchises deserve substantially better compensation.

Muscarello’s circumstances aren’t unusual. Professional cheerleaders across the NFL have frequently balanced practices, games, appearances and promotional commitments with full-time careers, education or other responsibilities. Cheerleading is a passion and a dream for many rather than a job capable of providing a primary income.

That reality has kept questions about NFL cheerleader pay alive for years. In 2014, a New York Jets cheerleader filed a lawsuit alleging she was paid just $3.77 per hour. A year later, an Associated Press investigation reported that some NFL cheerleaders were earning less than fast-food workers.

The issue has received renewed attention in recent years, particularly following the arrival of Netflix’s “America’s Sweethearts: Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders” in 2024.

The push for better pay is gaining momentum

The documentary series offered viewers an inside look at the intense audition process, training, rehearsals and performances required of Dallas Cowboys cheerleaders. It also showed members balancing their NFL ambitions with school, professional careers and personal responsibilities.

The increased visibility helped fuel further conversations about compensation. In 2025, Dallas Cowboys cheerleaders secured a reported 400% pay increase, marking a major development in the long-running fight for better wages.

The change has also demonstrated how compensation can vary between NFL franchises. Reports following the increase indicated that veteran Dallas Cowboys cheerleaders could earn around $75 per hour under the new pay structure, depending on their assignments and schedules.

Still, a significant issue remains as cheerleaders are generally hired by individual NFL franchises rather than the league itself. That means teams have considerable control over their compensation and working arrangements, making league-wide changes more complicated.

Muscarello’s viral “double life” has become a reminder that the women performing under the stadium lights often have demanding careers away from football, too. As the 2026 NFL season gets underway, fans are increasingly asking whether those contributions are being valued fairly.

articles.title: NFL admits the referees favored Broncos in win over the Rams
articles.standfirst: The league acknowledged the penalty that extended Denver’s winning drive shouldn't have been called
articles.summary: The league acknowledged the penalty that extended Denver’s winning drive shouldn't have been called
articles.body:
The Los Angeles Rams already knew the final minutes of their loss to Denver Broncos had turned on one controversial flag. What they learned afterward was that the league agreed with them.

Coach Sean McVay said the NFL told the Rams that Josh Wallace shouldn't have been called for defensive pass interference on a late fourth-quarter play that erased his interception and kept the Broncos’ game-winning drive alive.

“They agreed with me,” McVay said Wednesday. The sequence came with Los Angeles leading 26-23 and Denver facing third-and-6 in the red zone.

Bo Nix threw toward Pat Bryant near the right sideline, and Wallace appeared to come down with the interception. Then came the flag.

Call completely changed the final minute

The penalty wiped out Wallace ’s interception and gave Denver a fresh set of downs.

Six plays later, Nix scored to put the Broncos ahead 30-26 with 47 seconds remaining. The Rams got the ball back but could not produce a final answer.

The frustration around the call only grew when Bryant later acknowledged that he made sure the contact looked obvious enough to draw a flag.

“It was a little pass interference, I did sell it just enough to get the flag,” Bryant told CBS Colorado. “He definitely gave me a little nudge that I felt, I felt like I couldn’t get the ball so it was either the ball or the call and we ended up with the call.”

Asked whether there is an art to selling contact in football, Bryant didn't shy away from the idea.

“Oh, yeah, of course,” he said. “It’s something that a lot of people do in this league.”

Wallace , unsurprisingly, saw the play differently: “It was very frustrating,” he said after the game.

McVay refuses to let mistake define loss

The NFL’s admission gives the Rams some vindication, but McVay has made a point of not turning the officiating error into an excuse: “We’re not going to play the victim,” he said earlier in the week.

Los Angeles had several chances to take control before the controversial finish. The Rams blew a 16-0 halftime lead, committed other costly penalties and allowed Denver to seize momentum after Matthew Stafford threw a pick-six.

McVay said the real value of the league’s feedback is in how it helps coaches instruct players going forward.

“The goal is just to get good, consistent feedback,” he said. “The only thing that matters to me is how to educate my players.”

He also made clear that Wallace ’s technique was not something he intended to change based on the play. The damage, however, is already done.

Denver improved to 2-1, while the Rams dropped to 1-2 after a game in which one of the biggest moments was ultimately officiated incorrectly.

The league’s admission cannot rewrite the result. It does confirm that Los Angeles had every reason to question the call that helped decide it.
